metadata.title: Hierarchical process-level generative reward modeling with adaptive long-horizon reasoning for robust LLM alignment
metadata.abstract_summary: Composes a reward model from three tiers (long-horizon reasoning, step-level verification, integrated judgment) and bounds adversarial-response detection by the number of verification checkpoints and reasoning depth.

sections.heading: Claims
sections.text:
What the paper proposes or defines, as extracted (section, page):
- **Three-tier hierarchical verification composition** (category B) - Three sequential tiers—long-horizon internal reasoning, step-level verification with correctness labels, and integrated judgment—compose into one reward model that localizes errors and resists manipulation. (section 4.4. Hierarchical process-level generative reward models, p. 5)
  > Tier 1 provides the global context absent from process models, Tier 2 adds the step boundaries missing from unstructured GenRMs
- **Hierarchical annotation pipeline with quality filters** (category B) - A pipeline that has a strong reasoning model draft traces, a verifier model label each step, and filters retain only consistent, high-confidence annotations. (section 6.1. Hierarchical data generation, p. 6)
  > Quality filters retain instances where step labels are consistent with the final preference, the trace shows self-reflection markers
- **Adaptive depth allocation** (category C) - Per-instance token budgets for reasoning and verification are predicted from uncertainty, giving easy tasks shallow passes and hard tasks deep analysis. (section 6.3. Adaptive depth allocation, p. 7)
  > easier instances receive shallow reasoning and harder instances receive extended analysis
- **Multi-objective SFT with curriculum RL** (category C) - Joint supervised training over all tiers followed by reinforcement learning progressing from step correctness to trajectory coherence to preference. (section 6.2. Multi-objective training, p. 7)
  > The SFT loss jointly optimizes all hierarchical components

  > Process-level: step accuracy, error localization (F1), explanation quality (ROUGE-L), and process coherence.

concepts.name: Hierarchical annotation pipeline with quality filters

sections.heading: Method
sections.text:
- **Three-tier hierarchical verification composition**: Tier 1 T𝜃 emits 1000–2000-token internal reasoning; Tier 2 P𝜃 splits it into K≤20 tuples (step𝑘, V𝑘, exp𝑘); Tier 3 J𝜃 combines trace, step proportion 1/𝐾 ∑𝑘 V𝑘, and explanations. HPR𝜃(𝑥, 𝑦𝑎, 𝑦𝑏) = 𝐽𝜃◦𝑃𝜃◦𝑇𝜃(𝑥, 𝑦𝑎, 𝑦𝑏).
- **Hierarchical annotation pipeline with quality filters**: Sample M=10 traces from 𝜋reasoning; keep the longest trace whose judgment matches ground truth (Eq. 19); annotate each of K steps with 𝜋verifier (Eq. 20); filter on label–preference consistency, self-reflection markers, Kmin=5, confidence>0.8, retaining 50%–60%.
- **Adaptive depth allocation**: Uncertainty U(𝑥, 𝑦𝑎, 𝑦𝑏) = [H(p), 1−maxₛ p(s), 1−Aens] from a 100-token shallow prediction and K=4 agreement; MLP(3,256,2) outputs depths normalized to budget B and clipped: 𝐷internal = clip(𝐵⋅𝐷̃internal∕(𝐷̃internal+𝐷̃process), 500, 2500).
- **Multi-objective SFT with curriculum RL**: Loss (21) weights α1=0.2, α2=0.3, α3=0.25, α4=0.1, α5=0.15 across trace, step, label, explanation, preference terms; then PPO phases with ε=0.2 and KL penalties βstep=10−3, βtraj=5×10−4, βpref=10−4 decreasing.
- **Multi-granularity orchestration metric suite**: Process-level: step accuracy, error localization F1, ROUGE-L, coherence; outcome: preference accuracy, ECE; robustness: held-out accuracy, reward-hacking resistance, adversarial robustness, sampling stability; efficiency: tokens/query, uncertainty–depth correlation, speedup versus fixed depth.
- **K·D verification-checkpoint robustness bound**: Under Assumptions A.3–A.4, P(𝐸hack) ≤exp(−𝛼⋅𝐾⋅𝐷∕𝜎2); with average step-failure correlation 𝜌, replace K by 𝐾eff = 𝐾∕(1+(𝐾−1)𝜌), preserving monotonicity in K·D.

sections.heading: Evidence & Limits
sections.text:
- Evidence the authors report:
  - Three-tier hierarchical verification composition: Table 7 ablation: full hierarchy reaches 82.3% RM-Bench, 89.1% MATH-500, 58.3% AlpacaEval2 versus 74.2% for Tier 1 alone.
  - Hierarchical annotation pipeline with quality filters: Cross-verifier Cohen's κ=0.81 on 200 MATH-500 items; filter ablation varies RM-Bench accuracy by ±1.5%; 1500-instance audit finds 90.0% step-label accuracy.
  - Adaptive depth allocation: Table 5: 1820 versus 2100 tokens/query (13.3% saving), 1.15× speedup, uncertainty–depth correlation 0.78; hard-quartile accuracy 86.9% versus 87.2% fixed.
  - Multi-objective SFT with curriculum RL: Table 7: SFT+RL raises RM-Bench 78.5→82.3%, MATH-500 86.4→89.1%, AlpacaEval2 51.2→58.3% over SFT-only.
  - Multi-granularity orchestration metric suite: Tables 2–5 report all classes on MATH-500, RM-Bench, CodeContests, AlpacaEval2; HPR-GenRM reaches 89.1% step accuracy, F1 0.83, ECE 0.058.
  - K·D verification-checkpoint robustness bound: Fig. 6(b): detection rises 61.3% to 90.2% with K·D; Best-of-500 detection stays 88.4% at K=15, D=1500; measured ρ=0.12 gives 𝐾eff≈5.6.
- Limitations the authors state:
  - Three-tier hierarchical verification composition: Intended for offline reward labeling and batch RLHF; per-query latency of several seconds makes real-time use prohibitive without distillation.
  - Hierarchical annotation pipeline with quality filters: Verifier step depends on frontier APIs (GPT-4o or DeepSeek-R1); filtering discards 40%–50% of data; residual ~10% per-step annotation error floor.
  - Adaptive depth allocation: Trained post-hoc on 2K validation instances; accuracy drops 0.4–0.5%; transfer correlation falls to 0.71 and 0.69 on MATH-500 and CodeContests.
  - Multi-objective SFT with curriculum RL: No formal convergence proof for the three-phase curriculum; empirical convergence within 6 epochs; adds five loss weights and three KL penalties.
  - Multi-granularity orchestration metric suite: AlpacaEval2 win-ra

claims.text: Evidence the authors report:
Three-tier hierarchical verification composition: Table 7 ablation: full hierarchy reaches 82.3% RM-Bench, 89.1% MATH-500, 58.3% AlpacaEval2 versus 74.2% for Tier 1 alone.

Hierarchical annotation pipeline with quality filters: Cross-verifier Cohen's κ=0.81 on 200 MATH-500 items; filter ablation varies RM-Bench accuracy by ±1.5%; 1500-instance audit finds 90.0% step-label accuracy.
Adaptive depth allocation: Table 5: 1820 versus 2100 tokens/query (13.3% saving), 1.15× speedup, uncertainty–depth correlation 0.78; hard-quartile accuracy 86.9% versus 87.2% fixed.
Multi-objective SFT with curriculum RL: Table 7: SFT+RL raises RM-Bench 78.5→82.3%, MATH-500 86.4→89.1%, AlpacaEval2 51.2→58.3% over SFT-only.
Multi-granularity orchestration metric suite: Tables 2–5 report all classes on MATH-500, RM-Bench, CodeContests, AlpacaEval2; HPR-GenRM reaches 89.1% step accuracy, F1 0.83, ECE 0.058.
K·D verification-checkpoint robustness bound: Fig. 6(b): detection rises 61.3% to 90.2% with K·D; Best-of-500 detection stays 88.4% at K=15, D=1500; measured ρ=0.12 gives 𝐾eff≈5.6.
Limitations the authors state:
Three-tier hierarchical verification composition: Intended for offline reward labeling and batch RLHF; per-query latency of several seconds makes real-time use prohibitive without distillation.

Hierarchical annotation pipeline with quality filters: Verifier step depends on frontier APIs (GPT-4o or DeepSeek-R1); filtering discards 40%–50% of data; residual ~10% per-step annotation error floor.
Adaptive depth allocation: Trained post-hoc on 2K validation instances; accuracy drops 0.4–0.5%; transfer correlation falls to 0.71 and 0.69 on MATH-500 and CodeContests.
Multi-objective SFT with curriculum RL: No formal convergence proof for the three-phase curriculum; empirical convergence within 6 epochs; adds five loss weights and three KL penalties.
Multi-granularity orchestration metric suite: AlpacaEval2 win-rate variance is largest (SD = 1.2%) due to GPT-4 judging sensitivity to prompt phrasing.

K·D verification-checkpoint robustness bound: Assumes conditionally independent step failures and Gaussian noise; correlated failures weaken the bound; idealized form overestimates robustness by ~2.7× in the exponent.
Limitations they do not state: not assessed. Results are the authors' own, from their simulations, benchmarks or surveys; none evaluates delegation to cheaper models on software work.
